description: We are TRIAEGIS - a team passionate about space science, combustion research, and computational innovation. Our project, NextBurn: Flame in Freefall, explores how flames behave in microgravity through computational modeling, simulation, and scientific analysis. By investigating flame dynamics beyond Earth's gravity, we aim to advance our understanding of combustion, contribute to safer space exploration, and inspire innovative approaches to fire safety in space.
summary:
NextBurn: From Evidence Gap to Test Plan

How do we protect astronauts from fires in environments where critical safety conditions remain largely untested?

Developed by Team TRIAGIS for NASA's Flame in Freefall challenge, NextBurn is an evidence-driven fire-safety research platform designed to identify critical gaps in combustion testing for future Moon and Mars habitats.

Using 313 experimental test points from 14 NASA-related sources, NextBurn maps existing flame-test coverage across oxygen concentrations, atmospheric pressures, and gravity conditions. Our analysis reveals that only 1 of 24 lunar-gravity testing bins has direct evidence, while all 24 Martian-gravity bins lack direct tests for thin fabrics.

NextBurn combines interactive coverage maps, Bayesian modeling, and intelligent experiment prioritization. Rather than generating unsupported predictions, our model explicitly acknowledges uncertainty and declines when evidence is insufficient. Our four highest-priority proposed experiments are estimated to reduce weighted uncertainty by 73.2%.

Through an interactive, browser-based Coverage Console, NextBurn transforms fragmented NASA research into traceable scientific insights and actionable experimental priorities.

Our vision is simple: Safer space exploration begins with knowing what we still need to test.
details:
What it does and how it works NextBurn shows which fire-safety tests are missing for future Moon and Mars habitats, and which test to run next. It borrows from chip design verification, where you measure which conditions your tests have never reached and then write tests to fill those gaps. It works in six steps:

  1. We built a ledger of 313 flame-test points from 14 public NASA sources. Every row cites its source.
  2. We defined the conditions that matter: station air, plus the 34% and 37% oxygen atmospheres at 8.2 psia, each at lunar (0.16 g) and Mars (0.38 g) gravity.
  3. We divided those conditions into bins and marked each one as tested, tested only nearby, or never tested.
  4. We fitted a Bayesian model of whether a material keeps burning. It refuses to answer where there is no real test close by.
  5. We ranked the next tests by how much uncertainty each one removes.
  6. We froze our predictions for NASA's FM2 lunar burns, with a published hash, before any FM2 results exist.

Benefits It shows the gaps plainly. For thin fabrics, none of the 24 condition bins at Mars gravity has a test. Only one of the 24 bins at lunar gravity is tested. The model declines to answer on 96% of the map instead of guessing. The first recommended test, a parabolic flight at Mars gravity with 37% oxygen and 8.2 psia, removes 45.3% of the weighted uncertainty. Four tests remove 73.2%. Everything is reproducible: one setup command reruns the experiments, checks the prediction hash and rebuilds the dashboard.

Intended impact We want test programs to spend scarce flight and parabolic-flight time where it reduces risk the most, instead of on fixed test grids. In a simulation, choosing tests by uncertainty needed a median of 11 tests, against 24 for a fixed test matrix. Engineers who choose materials for habitats would get an honest answer to one question: "Has this been tested here, and if not, what should we test next?"

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Python with numpy, scipy and matplotlib for data parsing, coverage analysis, the Bayesian model, the test planner and the simulations.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the NextBurn Coverage Console. It's a single web page with ten tabs and 115 editable settings, plus an optional local server that reruns the scripts.
  • Node.js for page checks, and git with GitHub Pages for hosting.
  • Data: NASA PSI tables, which have no documented API, so we downloaded and parsed them; NTRS reports; and NESC TB 26-05.
  • Microsoft Copilot for research, coding help, data extraction, drafting and first-pass audit checks. The deck's cover image is AI-generated.
  • No special hardware. It runs on an ordinary computer.

How it's creative We took the coverage-closure method from chip design verification and applied it to spacecraft fire safety. The model is built to say "I don't know". A rule stops it from contradicting a real test, which we added after our first run did exactly that. We also made falsifiable predictions before the flight. Our own data audit scored 97.2% against a 98% bar we set in advance, and we report it as a fail on the front page.

Factors we considered

  • Data quality and where each number comes from: we checked the ledger with AI checkers, then a team member re-checked the disputed fields.
  • Sparse and inconsistent data: no PSI table states pressure, so those rows can't be used by the model yet.
  • Honesty about the model's weak spots: only 3 of its 23 observations didn't burn.
  • Keeping our own results checks separate from blind predictions.
  • Open, reproducible code, and independence from NASA: no logos and no implied endorsement

    Our Vision

Most scientific systems ask: What can we predict from the data we have?

NextBurn asks a different question: What critical evidence are we missing, and which experiment should come next?

By combining NASA research, transparent scientific modeling, and intelligent experiment planning, Team TRIAGIS aims to contribute to safer, more evidence-informed human space exploration.

NextBurn — Because the future of space safety depends not only on what we know, but on what we choose to test next.
